dashboard.guide_section_title: How to Perform an Accurate Crop Inspection
dashboard.guide_section_subtitle: Follow these three standard agronomic steps for reliable field detection.
dashboard.guide_step1_desc: Hold steady 10–25 cm away from the insect or damage in diffused natural light. Check both upper and underside leaf surfaces.
dashboard.guide_step2_desc: Our color-corrected YOLO11 detector calculates calibrated bounding boxes and classifies pests across 102 taxonomic categories.
dashboard.guide_step3_desc: Follow monitoring and cultural sanitations first. Only consider certified, crop-specific chemical treatments if damage exceeds economic thresholds.

ipm.general_warning_desc: This AI prediction indicates visual pattern similarity and is not a confirmed biological diagnosis. Please confirm the insect and crop identity in your field before taking any pest control action.
card1_default: Look for pests and damaged leaves regularly.
Check both the upper and lower surfaces of leaves.
Count affected plants or leaves across different spots.
Do not spray pesticides just because one insect is visible.
card2_default: Remove heavily infested plant parts when appropriate.
Keep field boundaries and surroundings free of weed hosts.
Follow recommended fertilizer and irrigation practices to keep plants strong.
Use crop rotation and other suitable cultural practices when appropriate.
card3_default: Protect beneficial insects and natural predators like spiders and ladybugs.
Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum pesticide use that kills helpful insects.
Consider eco-friendly biological pest control like neem sprays when suitable.
Remember that not every insect found in a field is harmful.
card4_default: First check whether pest damage is serious enough to require treatment.
Prefer suitable non-chemical methods whenever possible.
If pesticide treatment is necessary, use only a product registered and recommended for this crop.
Follow the product label and advice from a qualified agricultural expert; never invent dosages.
ipm.step1_desc: Walk your field twice a week. Count damaged leaves across 10–20 plants. If damage is light, allow natural predators to manage the pest.
ipm.step2_desc: Hand-pick damaged leaves, clear weed borders, and install sticky/light traps or botanical neem spray before considering chemicals.
ipm.step3_desc: If pest damage is spreading quickly or you are unsure about the insect, consult your local Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or extension officer.

guide.header_desc: Scientific pest diagnosis requires field corroboration. Use this evidence-conscious framework to validate visual AI detections and avoid premature pesticide applications.
guide.eil_heading: Visual Detection Does Not Mean Automatic Intervention
guide.eil_desc: In modern Integrated Pest Management (IPM), seeing an insect in a trap or on a leaf does not automatically justify chemical treatment. Treatment is only economically warranted when pest density crosses the Economic Threshold (ET)—the point where expected crop loss exceeds the cost of intervention.
guide.tip1_desc: Direct high-noon sunlight creates harsh specular highlights that blow out fine insect wing and antenna details. Scout in diffused morning light (8:00 AM – 10:30 AM) or overcast conditions for maximal neural feature visibility.
guide.tip2_desc: Insects are 3-dimensional organisms. A dorsal (top) view may misclassify an Asiatic rice borer as a yellow borer. Capture dorsal, lateral (side), and host-symptom context photos to evaluate species morphology.
guide.tip3_desc: Sap-sucking hemipterans and phytophagous mites congregate primarily on the abaxial (underside) surfaces of leaves to avoid solar heat and rain. Invert leaves gently to inspect colonies.
guide.helpline_desc: Connect directly with state agricultural university extension agronomists or government crop protection departments for certified chemical spray advisories and emergency pest management.
